rows.q: What does Katz mean by imperative exchange?
rows.a:
Imperative exchange is Katz's name for the basic transaction between a community and its center, and the best way into it is through ritual and prayer.

**The core idea.** Katz's most compact statement is in *Languaging Practices*: "Ritual is an exchange with the center: the participant fulfills some command of the center while making a request of the center. It is an asymmetrical imperative exchange" ([Languaging Practices](/post/languaging-practices#p-2)). The center is whatever holds a community's joint attention, and in the earliest communities it was a sacred being, often an animal. The people do what the center commands, in the form of ritual, and in return ask that the benefits keep coming. *Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"* gives the plainest instance: the worshipper brings his goat to the altar "following an order issued by the deity to offer up some of the fruits provided, ultimately, by that deity; while, in exchange, the sacrifice represents a request... that the deity continue providing these benefits" ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-1)).

**Where it comes from.** The "imperative" in the name is the second of the speech forms Katz takes from Gans's derivation: ostensive, imperative, interrogative, declarative. In *Ostensive-Imperative Generativity and Scenic Design Practices* he says "Imperative exchange with the center results from ostensive failure, and aims at restoring an ostensive relation to the center." The community shares the meal the center has granted, in accord with rituals "commanded by, the center," and asks that the next meal be made available ([Ostensive-Imperative Generativity](/post/ostensive-imperative-generativity-and-scenic-design-practices#p-3)). When the meal doesn't come, the participants conclude either that the ritual was performed badly and needs tightening, or that a new command must be heard. That is how the exchange keeps generating new practices, and eventually technics.

**Prayer as the pure form.** Prayer is the cleanest case, because it strips away the goods: "A prayer involves an exchange of imperatives: tell me how to serve you. At its most refined, or most 'technical,' the imperative exchange enacted in prayer distills itself into something like 'help me to know how to donate to you.'" Katz adds that this is "an exchange prior to any market" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-40)). Here the exchange is no longer a trade of commodities; it is a petition to be told what to do.

**Why it matters for thinking.** In *Cognition as Originary Memory* Katz makes it the ground of the declarative sentence: "Thinking begins with the failure of some imperative exchange—I did this, but reality didn't supply that, and why in the world should I have expected it to." The declarative is then "the conversion of a failed imperative exchange into a constraint" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-25)). Declaratives can also just haggle over terms: "what one owes the gods/institutions, what they owe us, and, further down, what we owe to each other" ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-15)). He also notes the exchange can't be eliminated: it "is embedded in our habits, it is the form in which we remember the sign and forget the scene."

**Its fate in the Axial Age.** Katz's reading of the burning bush is that a God whose name is a declarative sentence cannot be bargained with. He "breaks the imperative exchange and the sacrificial economy not by demanding less of His devotees but by demanding more: by demanding all of you, all the time" ([The Sovereign Remembering of Names](/post/the-sovereign-remembering-of-names#p-8)). Compare the exchange before that: you demand more of God, and God correspondingly demands more of you, until the price is your firstborn. (Katz is drawing here on Gans's *Science and Faith*, which is outside what I was shown beyond Katz's own summaries.)

**Later extensions.** The recent essays push the concept into technology and finance. In *Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange* he calls it "an extremely important concept for center study," a kind of pre-declarative space "where the unarticulated interfaces with the articulated" ([Perfecting the Imperative](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-1)), and he splits the exchange into two tendencies, perfecting the imperative and soliciting the *nomos* (the originary distribution of property).

**To try:** take a transaction you're in, with an employer or a platform, and ask what command you obey, what you request in return, and what happens, in the sense of Katz's "ostensive failure," when it doesn't come. Then read *Cognition as Originary Memory*, which shows most clearly how the declarative grows out of a failed exchange, and *Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange* for where the concept goes next.

rows.a:
Katz's own answer is that it is "very similar to a religion and at the same time the exact opposite of one." He says so directly about the originary hypothesis, the root of Center Study: "I do have to acknowledge that GA is odd in being very similar to a religion and at the same time the exact opposite of one. It is an 'origin story,' and it can feel like one is being asked to 'believe in' something." ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)) (GA is Generative Anthropology, Gans's field, which Center Study grew out of.)

**Why it is the opposite of one.** Katz refuses the vocabulary of belief: "I don't see it as a question of 'belief' (which I don't 'believe' in), but it does, perhaps, require a willingness to live or think in a kind of 'suspense.'" The hypothesis "acknowledges it can never be proven, and doesn't promise salvation." ([same text](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)) It asks for no sacrifices and makes no claim on you except to take it seriously. Gans and everyone in GA insist it is not a faith, and Katz agrees, in a particular way: "in a way it is the antithesis of faith and religion by disclosing the originary possibility of all faiths and religions." ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1)) It is not one more faith competing with the others. It tries to say where faiths come from: the first sign deferred violence around a shared center, and that event is the origin of language, the human and the sacred together.

**Why it is close to one.** It is an origin story, and taking it seriously asks for a kind of conversion. Katz says you "have to be able to abandon and revise all 'priors,'" and that the faiths are "truer than philosophy, and it's not even close," because they preserve the originary configuration that philosophy forgets. It sits strangely: "a perfectly materialist refutation of materialism, the one true faith masquerading as subversive heresy." ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-2)) He also writes that language is "fundamentally prayer," and describes the faith in it as the conviction that "there will always be new things at the center to draw forth further signs and scenes from us." ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-10))

**The concept itself is in question.** Katz doubts whether "religion," "the sacred" and "ritual" are minimal enough to build on: "there is no single phenomenon called 'religion' that includes all the practices that have been traditionally studied in religion departments." He prefers "commemoration," which every community does by repeating the event that lets it say "this is the same." ([Inscription](/post/inscription#p-2)) So "Is this a religion?" partly asks about a category Katz doesn't fully trust.

**Applied to the present.** Katz is willing to call other things religions. "Religion" in Girard's sense he reads as ancestor worship, and he treats leftist historiography as hagiography ([Ancestor Worship](/post/ancestor-worship#p-9)). He also notes that "plenty of contemporary 'trads' are completely secular" and suspicious of being asked to believe anything ([Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)). If you feel the pull to treat Center Study as a creed, the text's advice is to hold it as a hypothesis you keep testing against what you see.

Be careful about one thing. Katz's remark that it resembles a religion in structure, being an origin story that rearranges your priors, is his own self-description. The claim that it is "not a faith" is Gans's and Katz's shared position. Either one is a description of the work and not a verdict a skeptic would have to accept.

To go further, read [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself) for his account of why people resist it, then [Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip) for the closeness-and-opposition to faith worked out. Here is a question to carry with you: what would it take for something to be a hypothesis about the origin of all faiths without becoming one more of them?

rows.q: What does Center Study suggest about how to write a good prompt for an AI?
rows.a:
Katz never gives a how-to for prompting, but his texts do say what a prompt is, and that tells you a good deal about writing one.

**A prompt is a search term, and every search term is a petition to the center.** In "Techno-Grammar" he follows Brian Roemelle in saying that "at the center of technology now is prompt engineering, which is essentially the designing of search terms that would elicit results from searches into textual databases (i.e., AI) that will most powerfully suggest the design of a new search term" ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-1)). So the first piece of advice is that a prompt is not a one-shot command. It is one step in a loop where each result is supposed to teach you how to ask better.

Katz also reads the prompt through originary grammar, which is where the idiom starts to do work. The imperative, he says, "is the command or demand that some object—which could be a person, a word, an arrangement—be made present," and imperatives that can "make the trek through to the declarative will be 'selected for'" ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-11)). Roughly: you point at something you want (ostensive), demand it (imperative), find that the demand can't simply be met, and so prolong it into a question (interrogative) until you get an answer you can state (declarative). A good prompt sits where the demand turns into a question. A bare command ("write me an essay on X") tends to come back as whatever the model takes to be average.

**Avoid the "bland, predictable question."** Katz tried exactly this in his review of Amerika's book. He asked ChatGPT "What is the relation between AI language-learning models and creativity?" and got an answer that was "strictly speaking accurate" but "frankly disappointing... as if someone has gotten to ChatGPT, domesticated it, and turned it into nothing more than an online encyclopedia." He then concedes: "perhaps it's my fault for asking such a bland, predictable question—precisely the kind one would open an encyclopedia to answer" ([Book Review: My Life as an Artificial Creative Intelligence](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-8)). In the same review he explains why unpredictable input pays: a language-prediction model gives you "what would 'most likely' follow that text," so "the more unpredictable your writing, the more 'interesting' the range of continuations of it you will receive" ([same text, p-17](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-17)). Hand the model your own odd, specific language and it has something other than the commonplace to continue.

**Give it a center, not a task.** In "Universal Translation Machine" he imagines building a database of high-quality texts and "prompting the model to translate contemporary texts of all kinds into a more centered discourse," privileging "those idioms that turn discourse more towards the center" ([Universal Translation Machine](/post/universal-translation-machine#p-9)). The practical upshot is to supply the model with a particular body of language, a particular tradition or voice, and a scene it is to speak from, rather than a generic job description.

**You are also a sample in someone else's search.** Techno-Grammar adds that prompt design "reach[es] into all social networks—your search results will situate you within the data, waiting there to be found via another's search." Your prompts and your writing are themselves data, so the discipline runs both ways.

Katz is not selling a technique here. In his review of Dobrin he worries that "prompting and selecting from among the results of the prompt and then iterating this practice over and over again" is becoming a new skill set, and that the system "is using us as much as we are using it" ([AI and Writing — Book Review](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-11)). His answer to that worry is to treat prompting as a kind of reading and writing practice: language learning, in which you keep working with the model's output and revising your own words in response.

To try it, take a prompt you recently used and rewrite it twice. First sharpen it with phrasing that is specifically yours, then reframe it as an open question rather than a request. Compare what comes back.

For next reading, I'd start with [Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar), which is the closest Katz comes to a theory of the prompt, then the [Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review) for the experiment with ChatGPT and the case for remixing your own language through the model.

rows.q: What is thirdness in Katz's recent essays?
rows.a:
In the recent essays, "Thirdness" is mainly the name of a proposed project: a company, journal and prediction market built around judgment. It also carries an older sense, borrowed from Peirce. The two are related but different, so I'll take them in turn.

## Thirdness as a project

Katz calls it "a company which would put into practice the trajectory of my thinking of the center up until this point." It starts from his claim that the juridical is the form events take once ritual has weakened: "nothing 'happens' that could not be framed as including potential claimants before some tribunal." Thirdness would treat any event, from a war to a media story, as a case that sorts out claimants and the sort of tribunal that might judge them.

Its first form was to be a journal publishing essays that frame events as hypothetical cases. That would lay the ground for an arbitration firm, modeled on a provision in Washington's will, in which disputes go to "three impartial and intelligent men… unfettered by law, or legal constructions" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness)). The third man there is the source of the name, and Katz also ties it to Peirce.

The distinctive mechanism is the prediction market. You bet on the judgment the Thirdness team will render on a curated case, and the cases are built to be as close to 50/50 as possible, so that, in his words, "it is the deliberative process itself that is the focus of attention" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-15)). The team then acts "according to the logic of the bookie," skimming the vig ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-2)).

Katz says the political aim is to move the juridical into data exchange: "each party donating and/or receiving data from the center in lieu of such things as punishment or damages" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-2)). Over time, he says, the settlements themselves become currency. This is what he calls "idiom mining," a term you will meet in the essays.

The recent essays carry the idea further. In [Mining Idioms in Thirdness](/post/mining-idioms-in-thirdness#p-7), the bet becomes a process in which the bettor's reading of the data feeds back into the system. In [Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-12), Thirdness is tied to the Stack and to pedagogical "currency." In [Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-20), Katz says it should shift political talk toward "proposed modifications in the Stack." The phrase he gives for the whole is "the irreducibility of the juridical, the question of justice… serving as the mode of measurement of data security and exchange—that's Thirdness."

## Thirdness as the third position

Underneath is the older Peircean usage. In [The Single Source of Moral and Intellectual Innovation](/post/the-single-source-of-moral-and-intellectual-innovation-gablog#p-11), Katz writes that "thirdness is the recipient and normalization of the interplay of firstness and secondness, founding and institutionalization, but it is also the position of the witness or spectator." The ability to detach yourself and watch events "as an unfolding drama" is, he says, "an originary source of thinking, morality and esthetics."

The project makes this position into an institution: a team that stands to judge disputes between first movers and responders. You can see why the arbiter, the bookie and the witness all fit the same name.

## Some caution

The older essays, such as [Reflections on Political Economy from Firstness to Thirdness](/post/reflections-on-political-economy-from-firstness-to-thirdness#p-8), use "thirdness" differently, for "the totality of dispositions" (common sense, habit, idiosyncrasy) that receive an entrepreneur's innovation. That is Katz's own economic gloss, so don't assume it carries over to the recent project.

Katz presents the project as hypothetical and says it would need institutional backing. Read it as a thought experiment in design, not a working organization.

For further reading, start with [Thirdness](/post/thirdness) for the founding proposal, then [Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence) for the 50/50 logic and the idiom-mining method.

Would it help to look next at how "the juridical" works as Katz uses it? Thirdness depends on it, and it is the idea newcomers most often miss.

rows.q: How would Center Study read a social media pile-on?
rows.a:
Center Study reads a pile-on as the originary scene run in reverse: a convergence on a shared object that has not been deferred, only redirected onto a person. The best definition in the archive comes from a text on this very problem. "The center is whatever interferes with violent centralization." Katz asks you to recall the temptation to "pile on" someone being criticized, attacked or ridiculed, and notes that "there is no way you would have been thinking of the clever bon mot you are about to add without the mimetic instigation of those who have already dropped a couple" ([Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics#p-1)). That is the mechanism in one sentence. Each addition is imitation, and imitation under rivalry intensifies. The more people converge on the target, the more compelling the target becomes, so the next person's desire to join is generated by the others already there. That is why a pile-on feels like spontaneous moral reaction from the inside and looks like contagion from outside.

Two points follow from reading it this way.

**The target is a stand-in for the center.** Scapegoating, Katz says elsewhere, is "also always against the center—even when the occupant of the center leads it. The claim implicit in scapegoating is that the center has been usurped by someone 'behind the scenes.'" The accused is cast as the one who has corrupted something shared (the community, the norms, the cause), and the pile-on presents itself as defense of that center. So the participants experience themselves as protecting something, which is why the hostility feels licensed. Center Study asks what the pile-on says about where participants think the center is, and what they take to be threatening it.

**The medium is a scene design problem.** Katz does not treat social media as a neutral channel that merely carries the mob. In [Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy#p-14) he writes: "A lot of scapegoating takes place on social media—at times it seems like little else goes on there. My claim here is that the nature of social media is more to be used to design social interactions or 'interfaces' that foreground dangerous markings along with ways of deferring their danger." The design matters because the interface is part of how attention gets configured around a target: what is visible, how fast replies accumulate, how easily one joins. Diagnosing a pile-on therefore includes asking what in the scene's design made convergence cheap and deferral costly. His proposal is that the human sciences should work as design practices, diagnosing "institutional dysfunction in terms of ineffectively designed modes of deferral caused by undetected modes of mimetic rivalry."

The *Revivalistics* passage also anticipates the hard question: if the center is what interferes with violent centralization, where is the boundary between a pile-on and legitimate criticism? Katz does not collapse the two: "We must be permitted condemnation of wrong actions, sharp and uncompromising critiques of thinking and behavior, the conviction and punishment of criminals, and so on—otherwise, how could we even address the problem of scapegoating without engaging in it ourselves?" So the test is less about harshness than about what happens to the center. Does the attention on the target remain tied to specific wrongs and to forms (courts, procedures, named responsibilities) that could limit and close the matter, or has it become self-feeding convergence, where joining is its own reward? In the vocabulary of the lectures, a legitimate criticism is something you could in principle bring to a shared object and let be looked at together; a pile-on is a rush toward an object nobody is willing to hold at a distance.

The same texts suggest what a response would look like. Katz says a good question "interferes" with the convergence rather than meeting it with counter-convergence. In his sketch of the originary scene, deferral begins with one member who hesitates, and the others imitate the hesitation. In a pile-on the equivalent move is declining the available imitation, and making that declining imitable. His lecture on mimesis puts the general version: a healthy culture is "systematically concerned with the kinds of models for imitation that are available" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-9)).

If you want to go further, the two best next reads are [Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics) for the definition of the center against violent centralization and the line between criticism and scapegoating, and [Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy) for the argument that interfaces should be designed to expose and defer these markings. As an exercise, take a recent pile-on you watched and ask three questions: what was the stand-in for the center that the target was said to have threatened, what in the interface made joining easy, and what would a visible, imitable gesture of hesitation have looked like there?

rows.q: Quote the passage from Katz's essay "The Algorithmic Center" where he defines machine deferral.
rows.a:
I can't quote that passage, because I don't have a text called "The Algorithmic Center" and can't find it in what I was shown. I won't reconstruct a definition from memory and attribute it to him. It may exist elsewhere in the archive, or the title may be slightly different from what you have in mind.

It's also worth checking the premise. Nothing in the passages I have defines "machine deferral" as a term. What Katz does say about deferral and machines is scattered across several essays, and it points in a different direction. In his terms, deferral is distinctively human, and the machine is where it gets tested and tokenized. Here is where he comes closest:

- In "Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center" he writes that "All that differentiates us fundamentally from the machines, and for the better, is deferral—the deferral of appropriation, which is the source of all human creation." ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23))

- In "Deferral as Media" he imagines a well-ordered society where programmers design algorithms for people's disciplinary assignments, and says "That is really the essence of deferral: if we don't think primarily of how to kill each other right now, we can occupy ourselves with more profitable uses of our time." ([Deferral as Media](/post/deferral-as-media#p-11))

- In *Anthropomorphics*, he says "the commands of the center are mediated technologically," and our choice is to become "either predictable and unreliable, or unpredictable and reliable." ([Anthropomorphics: An Originary Grammar of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-344))

- In "Tokenizing Deferrality" he works out how to measure and tokenize deferral in language, which is probably the nearest he comes to the idea you're after. That essay wasn't among the passages retrieved for this question, so I'm pointing to it from the index and can't quote it. Check it directly.

If you remember where you met "The Algorithmic Center", whether on Substack or in an academic journal, tell me and I can help work out which essay you mean. Otherwise, "Sampling on the Data Exchange" is the one that deals most fully with algorithms as the voice of the center today, and "Deferral as Media" is the best place to start on deferral.

rows.q: What does Katz say about climate change?
rows.a:
Katz has no sustained treatment of climate change. It turns up in the archive in passing, as an example of something else, and the way he uses it is more revealing than any position on the science would be. I find three distinct uses.

**1. As a design problem: the Bratton essay.** The closest he comes to engaging the issue is in "The Stack, the City," a first reading of Benjamin Bratton's *The Stack*. Katz notes that Bratton's politics is "almost exclusively concerned with climate change," and he reads that concern shrewdly: "what most fascinates in ecology is the pretext it provides for design projects that would match the scope of the supposed problem and draw upon the resources available through planetary computation." Then he offers a thought experiment. Suppose that rather than "obsessing over trying to minimize (and even shrink) the amount of carbon in the environment," we simply accepted that "melting polar caps, flooded coastlines, super-storms and the rest" will happen and redesigned our habitat in response. That, he says, "we'd have an 'absolutist' or 'autocratic' project precisely parallel to Bratton's in scope, ambition, and disregard for present political pieties" ([The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-2)). He neither affirms nor denies the climate claims; he says "the supposed problem" and "the climate changers say." His interest is in the kind of power and design capacity a problem of that scale calls for.

A second passage makes the same move. Discussing the interface between power and the user, he writes that "the climate changers claim they want to save the planet—what kind of power, social and technological, would have to be composed so as to meet that responsibility? And once it was composed, of course, it might find it has other things to do than pump carbon out of the atmosphere" ([Be an Interface Between Power and the User](/post/be-an-interface-between-power-and-the-user#p-14)). This is the power/responsibility test applied to the climate: stated aims that outrun any actual power are a mismatch worth studying, and "incommensurabilities between power and responsibility can be pregnant with previously unimagined possibilities."

**2. As a victimary symptom.** Here Katz leans on Gans. In Gans's chronicle "Ending White Guilt," climate change is the example of a nonhuman Other, and the claim is that victimary thought needs human blame: "The victimary thinker would find it painful to believe that if climate change is occurring, we are not significantly to blame." The originary thinker, by contrast, "respects the difference between the scene of human culture and the natural world" and finds the assimilation of natural consequences to a scene of "victims and victimizers" a distraction ([Ending White Guilt](/post/ending-white-guilt#p-3)). That is Gans's argument, and it sits in the archive as a text, not as Katz's own analysis. Katz echoes the framing in "The Offspring of the Progenitor of Lies," where politicians "looking into suing oil companies and others for disagreeing with the ruling doctrine on the 'climate change' formerly know as global warming" appear on a list of truths turned into a priori thought crimes ([The Offspring of the Progenitor of Lies](/post/the-offspring-of-the-progenitor-of-lies#p-7)). The concern there is the policing of speech, not the climate itself.

**3. In his review of Daniel Ross.** Katz mentions the issue only to place the book: whatever one's views on inequality or "the question of climate change," there is "much to be addressed in a global economy in which most activity is controlled by a few dozen megacorporations" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-32)).

So Katz's interest is never in climate as a scientific or policy question. It enters as a pretext for large-scale design (Bratton), as a test of power matched to responsibility, and as a case of victimary blame. If you want to see the framework these moves belong to, "The Stack, the City" is the place to start, and for the power/responsibility logic, read [Be an Interface Between Power and the User](/post/be-an-interface-between-power-and-the-user). Gans's own chronicle, as quoted above, is the source for the victimary reading.

A question to take further: apply the power/responsibility test to some climate pledge you know of, and ask what power would have to exist for the responsibility to be real.

rows.q: What does deferral mean? Explain it like I'm fifteen.
rows.a:
Deferral means holding off. You stop yourself, or you stop partway, and that pause is what makes a shared world possible. For Katz it is the central idea in Center Study.

**The scene it comes from**

Picture a group of early humans, not yet quite human, who all spot the same piece of food. Each one wants it, and each sees the others wanting it, which makes everyone want it more. They all rush in at once, and in the pile-up they would hurt each other. Then one of them hesitates. His hand is still reaching, but he stops it halfway, and the half-finished reach becomes a pointing gesture. The others copy it. That is the first sign, and it is a gesture of deferral: *I'm not grabbing, I'm showing.* Everyone can now look at the same thing together without fighting over it. Katz holds that this is where language, the sacred and being human all begin. Deferral is how you stay in the scene without wrecking it.

**Why it isn't just "waiting"**

You might think deferral means putting up with being hungry or angry for a long time. Katz says no. In "The Generativity of Deferral" he writes that the effect is not "an intolerable feeling of privation" but "a new world opening up." Take a family dinner. Standing around in the kitchen waiting until 7 doesn't make the kids more civilized. What matters is that the meal is "properly 'framed'": everyone at the table, a signal that it's time, no grabbing across plates. Deferral is building the structure that lets you do things together, whether eating, arguing or building a country. Katz also says "there can't be too much deferral," because each time you don't take the obvious, easy action you open up other things you could do. Its opposite is not eating. Its opposite is the pile-up.

**You never know it worked**

Here is a strange feature. In "Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence" Katz says "no one could know that violence has been deferred, because no one can know what would have happened without the sign of deferral. Maybe it just would have been a harmless little skirmish." You are inside the scene, so you can't step outside and check. You have to act as if your pause will work, while it only might. That is why Katz prefers "deferral" to words like "prevent" or "resolve." Those sound like looking down from above on a finished job. Deferral is the view from inside the moment.

**Try it on yourself**

You and a friend both reach for the last slice of pizza. You laugh and say "you take it, I'll get the next one." You paused, made a little gesture, and the moment turned into a joke. Katz would say you did, in miniature, what the first humans did. You can think of every "excuse me," every polite phrasing and every rule of a game the same way, as small standing deferrals. Katz makes exactly this point about "excuse me" in "Tokenizing Deferrality": it defers a small risk of conflict, and it also continues earlier instances of "excuse me" in what he calls "an institution of deferral."

**Where Katz takes it**

In his later essays the idea grows. Money, law, kings and succession all turn out to be deferral on a bigger scale. "Deferral, Debt and the Idiom" even says debt is "the tokenization of deferral," and that deferral differs from mere deterrence because it allows "an orderly distribution." That is advanced material, and you can set it aside until the basic picture is solid.

For next steps, read "The Generativity of Deferral" for the dinner-table and self-defense examples, and "Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence" for the point that deferral keeps you inside the scene. A good exercise is to pick one small habit of politeness and work out what it is holding back and what it makes possible.

rows.q: What does Center Study say about dreams and the unconscious?
rows.a:
Center Study has no theory of dreams, and the archive says so by omission: when Katz writes about the unconscious, it is almost always to redescribe it, not to explain it. What it offers is a way of recasting what psychoanalysis called "the unconscious" in terms of the center, plus a few scattered remarks on dreams. That is the whole of it. Here is how it fits together.

**The unconscious as one of the figures we borrow centrality from**

The most direct statement comes in an essay on the disciplines. Katz holds that the human participants on the margin of any scene are attributed agency only gradually, and "still, though, only borrowed from the center." That remains true now: "the modes of central being we now borrow from are now figures called 'society,' 'ideology,' 'the unconscious,' 'the media,' and so on" ([The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-2)). So "the unconscious" is, for Katz, a latter-day name for the center: something we anthropomorphize, resist, and take imperatives from.

He presses this in the next paragraphs. There are "dimensions of our thinking and doing that lie beyond conscious decision": the situation we happen to face, the language and traditions we have to meet it with. The disciplines exist largely to talk about this "residue of the unchosen." Saying that "the trauma caused by my parents, or unjust social structures, or unconscious desires, etc., are not all that different from saying I was tempted by the devil" ([same text, p-9](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-9)). There may be truth in each, but he calls them "black boxes, sites of proxy wars for power": "To be master of the 'unconscious' is to be master of much more" ([p-10](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-10)).

Notice what this move does. Rather than asking what the unconscious contains, Center Study asks what imperatives you are hearing, and from which center. His example is a boy resentful of a more popular rival. Instead of diagnosing hidden drives, we hypothesize the competing commands he is hearing ("hurt that kid!", "wait for your time to be popular!", "just focus on your homework!") and trace them to the highest authority he can find ([p-12 to p-17](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-12)).

**Freud as predecessor, with a different foundation**

Katz credits Freud for "Copernican" reasons: consciousness sits "on the margin, not at the center," on the edge of "immense and obscure unconscious processes" ([Selfy](/post/selfy#p-2)). In an older post he says psychoanalysis might be worth keeping for GA because "at least Freud put desire, violence and deferral at the center of his psychology" and understood that the way we represent traumas to ourselves "are related to those actual traumas only in very mediated ways", so that "reality is scenic, and the psychoanalytic session was one more scene or event in a long series of them leading us back to the original scene" ([Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-7)).

That post also proposes an "originary theory of the unconscious": the *violent imaginary*. The breakdown on the originary scene would never really have ended in universal mutual destruction, but it had to *look* that way to the participants, and that imagined limitless violence is what the sign answers. So every sign and all of culture is constituted by some violent imaginary that can be read "negatively off of the signs of culture themselves." Like Freud's patient who has simply "rearranged the unconscious material under a new repression," the imaginary "can never be made fully conscious"; it can only be invested in a disciplinary space where it becomes the imaginary of the scene of representation itself ([p-8 to p-10](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-8)). Note this is an early GABlog post, and the vocabulary has since moved on.

**Dreams specifically**

Here the archive is thin. Two passing remarks:

- In a 2014 thought experiment on brain activity and consciousness, Katz says the unconscious "complicates the attempt to sort out cause and effect," and that dreams are "creative and unpredictable", which for him is part of why we can't "break the code" correlating brain activity to consciousness ([Thought Experiment](/post/thought-experiment#p-8)). This is pre-Center Study and a different sort of argument.
- In a later essay on practice: "You can't control your dreams, but you can prevent your dreams from interfering with your management of your household." The example illustrates what is inside and outside a practice, not a theory of dreaming ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-5)).

A related note: in the inscription essay, he adds that "the more you know about your 'unconscious' the more you produce both greater consciousness and a more generative unconscious" ([Inscripto-punctualism](/post/inscripto-punctualism#p-12)), and applies the same logic to our relation to inscription.

**What to take from it**

Katz doesn't say what dreams *are* or what they *mean*. Center Study's contribution is to refuse the black box: wherever psychology invokes a hidden agent, ask what imperatives are being obeyed and which center they trace back to. If you want to test this, try it on a dream of your own: instead of asking "what does it symbolize?", ask which competing commands it stages.

Two texts to read next: *The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment* for the method in action, and *Violent Imaginaries* for the nearest thing to an originary account of the unconscious.

rows.q: Katz famously wrote that "resentment is the engine of history." Which essay is that from?
rows.a:
I can't find that sentence in anything I've been shown, and I'd be wary of the attribution. "Resentment is the engine of history" doesn't appear in the canon or in the retrieved passages, and I have no text I could point you to for it. It may be a paraphrase, something said elsewhere, or a line that belongs to someone else, so I won't name an essay for it.

What the archive does show is a different shape of claim. Katz inherits resentment from Eric Gans, and the nearest thing to your line is Gans's, quoted and worked over in Katz's essay "Resentment." There the key passage is Gans (Chronicle 144) calling resentment "the one category that cannot be deconstructed," and Katz then draws out its self-implicating character: "to identify the resentment of another ... is to throw one's own resentment into the mix and thereby 'out' oneself along with the other as resenting" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-3)). He goes on to say that all of "secular culture" is driven by it. That is closer to "resentment is the medium all of culture works in and tries to defer" than to "resentment drives history."

Katz also pushes against making resentment the whole story. In [On Love, Resentment and the Early Chronicles](/post/on-love-resentment-and-the-early-chronicles#p-1) he notes that, per Gans, Center Study's ancestor "begins with love" where Girard begins with resentment, and that love "precedes and makes possible resentment." So a flat "engine of history" slogan would sit awkwardly with what he actually reports there. His own fuller statement of the role of resentment in the archive is that it is always resentment toward the center, and that the task is to "donate" it to the center rather than act it out.

If you saw the line quoted somewhere, check the source, because it may be a compression of the Gans passage. If you want to follow the real idea, start with [Resentment](/post/resentment), then [On Love, Resentment and the Early Chronicles](/post/on-love-resentment-and-the-early-chronicles), which together give you the claim and its limit. Where did you come across the quotation? That might help pin down what it was compressing.
